Please be informed that *sāmudrika* (physiognomy) is a principal branch of the science of astrology (*jyotiṣaśāstra*), through which the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of women and men can be properly understood. Within the science of astrology, there are two divisions known as *gaṇita* (mathematics) and *phalita* (interpretation of results). While all scholars accept *gaṇita* as true, many scholars do not accept *phalita* as true.

To me, even the results of palmistry appear to be true; however, for the purpose of explaining those results, it is first absolutely necessary to contemplate them. "He who declares the auspicious and inauspicious—having observed the horoscope without exception according to the differences of countries—his word shall not be false. (1)

For example, we shall here describe certain marks of men and women that have been tested on several occasions and found to be reliable. A man whose complexion is fair, whose body is slender, whose frame is delicate, and who has abundant hair on his wrists and shanks, is extremely lustful and possesses many sons.

One whose body is tall, whose complexion is like that of wheat, who is extremely clever, and whose body is emaciated, is either sonless or has very few offspring. One who has a short neck, a slender body, and a fickle nature is deceitful and treacherous. A man who is one-eyed, bald, lame, or cat-eyed is sinful, crooked, and untrustworthy.

He whose left side of the body is crooked will have daughters as his offspring, while he whose right side is crooked will possess a lineage of sons. Furthermore, one who has a tall stature, a large physique, speaks much, and utters loud sounds is proud and full of ego. One with a medium build, a heavy body, a fair complexion, and who speaks quickly, such that his tongue falters in speech [is also so characterized].

If there is a split in the teeth, he will certainly be a clever scholar, virtuous, and have many sons. If he is dark-complexioned, short-statured, ugly, and cruel-natured, he will inevitably be a liar, a deceiver, and a rogue. As is the conduct of a man, so is that of his wife; if a woman is short-bodied and has dark eyes, she is unchaste.

She whose second toe is longer than her big toe will be unchaste and a widow. She whose feet are greenish-yellow, heavy, with short toes, a somewhat stout body, a slender waist, and a fair complexion will likewise be promiscuous, shameless, and without a protector.

A woman who has long limbs and an emaciated body, whose hair grows on her ankles and wrists, and who walks so swiftly that her feet do not touch the ground in the middle of their stride, is also unchaste. One whose shoulders, breasts, hips, and gait are swaying, and who moves quickly and with a sidelong motion, is likewise unchaste. Through such characteristics, one’s disposition, virtues, vices, and lifespan can be discerned.
Through reflection upon and examination of the Sāṃkhya scriptures, one attains a correct knowledge of the characteristics of the body.

The *Rāganthaka* consists of two sections: 1) the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa* (First Section), and 2) the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* (Second Section). In the *Pūrvakhaṇḍa*, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the major and minor limbs of men, as well as the lines and marks on the palms, have been described in detail. In the *Uttarakhaṇḍa*, the characteristics of the major and minor limbs of women, as well as the lines and marks on the palms, have likewise been written in detail.

Now begins the *Sāmudrika-śāstra* together with its vernacular commentary (*bhāṣā-ṭīkā*). **Auspicious Invocation:** Having paid homage to Lord Gaṇeśa, to the Guru, and to the Lord of Girijā (Pārvatī), this commentary on the *Sāmudrika* has indeed been composed by Nārāyaṇa. (1)

Having offered salutations to Lord Gaṇeśa, the bestower of wealth and glory, and to my Guru-deva as well as Girijāpati (Mahādeva), Nārāyaṇaprasād Miśra has composed this vernacular commentary on the Sāmudrika treatise. Now, therefore, I shall fully expound the examination of the lines of the hand. For a man, the right hand is to be known [as significant], while for a woman, the left hand is auspicious. Meaning: Now, hereafter, we shall describe the consideration of the lines of the hand; listen to it.

One should examine the male characteristics in the right hand and, having examined the left hand, describe the female characteristics; through the lines of the hand, one should declare all auspicious and inauspicious results. (2) This Sāmudrika Tantra spoken by Śiva concerns the auspicious and inauspicious lines of the hand; by the mere knowledge of which, a person does not grieve. (3)

In the *Sāmudrika-śāstra* spoken by the illustrious Śiva (Mahādeva), the arrangement of auspicious and inauspicious [marks] according to the lines on the hand has been recorded; by thoroughly knowing that auspiciousness and inauspiciousness—that is, happiness and suffering—a person does not encounter sorrow, but rather remains happy. 3. *Sāmudrika-śāstra*. Royal Marks: If one possesses a powerful *rājayoga* at birth, [one attains royalty].

In the hand or the foot, a royal mark necessarily arises. (4) Meaning: For one at whose time of birth a powerful *rājayoga* occurs, there will certainly be royal marks such as the lotus on the hand or foot. (4) The line situated at the root of the ring finger is considered to be named *puṇya*; it extends from the middle finger to the end of the wrist. (5)

If there is a straight line at the base of the *anāmikā* (the finger between the little finger and the middle finger), it is auspicious and bestows merit; likewise, if there is a single straight and complete line extending from the middle finger to the *maṇibandha* (the wrist), that too is auspicious. ||5|| Similarly, lines resembling an elephant goad (*vaiśārana*) or a wind-shield (*vātavāraṇa*), or those for lifting up (*uddhāraṇa*), located in the middle of the right hand [are auspicious].

If there is a fish, an umbrella, an elephant, a lake, a goad, or a lute—whichever of these marks appears on the palm of one's right hand—that person shall become a king upon the earth. (6) Indeed, he whose palm is marked with a pestle, a club, a sword, and a plough becomes a lord of wealth; such is the fruit of a garland of flowers when one is born from a soil that yields kings. (7)

One whose hand is marked with the signs of a pestle, a mountain, a sword, or a plow shall certainly be wealthy; likewise, one who has the sign of a flower or a garland shall be wealthy, and if this mark appears on one born of a royal lineage, he shall become a king. (7) [With Hindi Commentary] Regarding the fruit of upward lines: A straight line, specifically, brings about the attainment of a kingdom.

8. Fragmented, it yields evil results; diminished, it yields diminished results. Meaning: An upward line that runs from the middle finger to the base of the hand as a single, unbroken line especially brings about the attainment of sovereignty. If the upward line is fragmented, it yields evil results; if it is diminished, it yields diminished results. 8. [The results of signs in the shape of barley.]

That mortal in whose middle of the thumb there shines a mark like that of a man, becomes illustrious; he is adorned as an ornament to his own lineage and is endowed with women, wealth, and various riches. (9) [The Sign of Attaining Prosperity]

On the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet of men, there appear the marks of the lotus, the man, the discus, the banner, the chariot, the throne, and the palanquin, just as on other limbs; where these signs are present, supreme Lakṣmī always dwells. (10) [The Marks of Imperishable Prosperity]

Whether it be a jar, a pillar, a horse, a drum, or a tree upon the palm or the sole of the foot of a man—if he is surrounded by unbroken prosperity, is he a scholar or a vintner? *The Science of Palmistry (Sāmudrika-śāstra)* Meaning: He upon whose palm or sole there are these marks—a jar, a pillar, a horse, a tree, or a staff—shall be endowed with undiminished fortune; otherwise, he will be either a learned man or a vintner (a seller of liquor).

11. The supreme marks of royalty: He who has a broad forehead, lotus-petal eyes, and a well-rounded head is a lord of the earth’s circle. Those great men say that he whose arms reach down to his knees is the foremost among kings. 12.

He whose head is large, whose eyes resemble lotus petals, and whose skull is beautiful and rounded, becomes the lord of the earth; and he whose hands reach his knees while standing upright becomes a preeminent king or a great monarch. (12) His navel is deep and straight, his nose is well-formed, his chest resembles the surface of a jeweled stone, and his feet are indeed reddish in hue and soft.

He shall become that best of kings. (13) Meaning: He whose navel is deep and whose nose is straight, whose chest is as pure as a slab of precious stone, and whose feet are soft and red in hue—he becomes a preeminent king. (13) If there is a mark on the hand or on the sole of the foot, or if there is a mole on the hand, it bestows incomparable wealth; likewise, such a mark on the soles of men’s feet bestows the happiness of riding upon vehicles. (14)

If there is a sesame-mark on the instep, it bestows immeasurable wealth; likewise, a sesame-mark on the sole of the foot grants the happiness of vehicles and riches. (14) [With the Bhāṣā-Ḍīkā]. For those born into royal lineages, such is the full result; for others, it becomes diminished, though the auspicious mark remains clearly visible. (15)

All these aforementioned marks bestow royal happiness in its entirety upon those born in the lineage of King Artharāja; for other men, they grant only minor results such as a home and prestige. (15) The Result of the Fish Line: He in whose hand there is a fish line attains success in his undertakings. He should be known as wealthy and possessed of many sons; of this there is no doubt. (16)

If a fish is seen held in the palm of one's hand, that person will possess success in their undertakings; that is to say, whatever business or other activities that person performs will be accomplished, and therein they shall obtain wealth, grain, and so forth. Furthermore, that person will become wealthy and have many sons—of this there is no doubt. (16) [Signs such as the balance: If a balance scale is seen in the middle of the hand, it indicates a village as well as a forest.

There is no doubt that for such a person, success in trade shall come to pass. (17) If, between the hands of a man, a scale (balance) appears, or if within a square line resembling a village or city, various colorful marks are perceived, and the mark of a thunderbolt (vajra) is seen, then for that person there is undoubtedly the attainment of *vāṇijya* (trade); that is, he shall become wealthy through commerce. (17) [Marks such as the lotus (*padma*) and others.]

A lotus, a bow, a sword, an octagon, and so forth are seen [on his hands]. Such a man, whether he be a woman or a man, shall be wealthy and happy. (18) **Meaning:** He in whose hand [are found] a lotus, a bow, a sword, an octagon, and so forth, according to the *Sāmudrika-śāstra* (the science of bodily marks), accompanied by its commentary...

If it appears in the *nihā* (the lower part of the hand), that person—whether woman or man—is wealthy and happy; that is, one who holds in his hand the signs of a spear (*śakti*), a lance (*barhīka*), or a javelin (*tomara*), as well as a sword (*khaḍga*). Furthermore, by the mark of a lotus, a man becomes a king and a woman a queen. When there is a configuration resembling a bow with a peculiar grip known as the "entrance of the plow" (*halapraveśa*), it is called a *tomara*.

If there is the mark of a bow, the person becomes an archer; if there is the mark of a sword, he becomes a warrior. If the hand appears in the shape of a sword or if the mark of an arrow is clearly visible in the center of the palm, he becomes a great hero who engages in battle. If there is the mark of eight corners, he is born into a royal family. If all three of these marks are present, a man attains a supreme kingdom; by being born with these, one becomes a king or a lord of the earth. (18)

If there is one mark, one attains an ordinary kingdom; with two marks—such as the conch and so forth—one enjoys sovereignty and royal power. If marks in the shape of a chariot, a discus, or a banner are seen, or if the shape of a conch, a discus, and a banner is visible on the nose, one attains a kingdom equal to that of Indra. (21) [With] the mark of a goad, that person becomes wise through the bestowal of all sciences. (19)

He upon whose palm there may be the mark of a goad, an earring, or a discus—whose kingdom shall be most excellent, according to the words of the *Sāmudrika*—and if a mark in the shape of a conch, a discus, or a banner should appear, as well as a mark in the shape of a nose, [he will possess] everything.

A person possessing these marks becomes wise and learned; furthermore, if one has all three signs—the goad, the earring, and the discus—on the palm of the hand, he becomes a knower of the Vedas and Vedānta. If the mark shaped like a nose is clearly visible, the man becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin); however, if there is only one such mark, he becomes proficient in worldly business and sciences. (19)

If there are two marks for the enjoyment of an ordinary kingdom, then there are some specific marks for a particular kingdom—the trident mark (*triśūla-cihna*). This is the word of Nārāyaṇa, who dwells in the Ocean of Milk, regarding the enjoyment of sovereignty. [22] The mountain-bracelet (*girikaṅkaṇa*) and other such marks: if the trident is in the middle of the hand, by that one becomes a king. The mountain-bracelet, the female organ (*yoni*), the human skull (*naramuṇḍa*), the jar (*ghaṭa*), and so forth—if these marks are indeed on the hand of a man during sacrifice, ritual action, charity, and the worship of gods and twice-born brahmins, he shall become a royal minister. [20]
23. If there is the mark of a trident between the hands, it should be known as a sign of becoming a king; that is to say, a pure trident is manifested between the hands of a man or a woman.

O Artha, if a person has the manifest marks of a mountain (giri), a bracelet (kaṅkaṇa), a vulva (yoni), a human skull (naramuṇḍa), and a jar (ghaṭa) on their hand, that man will certainly become a king if he is destined to be one. If there is doubt regarding the trident (triśūla)—that is, if it is not clearly manifest—then by taking refuge with a king, he shall enjoy royal pleasures or become a royal minister. If all three marks are present, he will certainly become a royal minister; and as for those who possess these... or [belong to] the king's...

Having become a government official (*karmacārī*), one should perform various kinds of sacrifices and give gifts. If all five marks are present on the palms, one becomes a great minister; if there are two or one mark, one becomes like a royal minister in terms of power and prosperity. One should worship the deities and the Brahmins. [The marks include] the sun, the moon, and other signs; the spear (*śakti*), the club (*tomara*), and so forth. If the spear, the club, and the arrow are clearly visible in the center of the palm, as well as the sun, the moon, the creeper-like eye, the eight-sided (*aṣṭakoṇa*) and the three-sided (*trikoṇaka*) figures, [then these qualities follow].

A man who has the shape of a chariot wheel as a mark on his hand would covet the kingdom of Indra. One who has the marks of a temple, an elephant, or a horse will become wealthy and happy. [From the *Sāmudrika-śāstra*: The meaning is that if even one of these marks—such as the sun, the moon, a creeper, an eye, an octagon, a triangle, a temple, an elephant, or a horse—is present upon a person's hand, that person will be wealthy and happy; if the mark of the sun is present, the person will be radiant.]

If the mark is that of the moon, his fame shall shine; if the mark is large, his glory shall spread throughout the world. If there be the marks of eight corners, three corners, or a temple, that man shall be a builder of wells, ponds, lakes, shrines, and palaces. If the mark be that of an elephant, horses shall be tied at his gate; if the mark be that of a horse, steeds shall be tethered at his door. ॥24॥

The mark of a barley grain: He in whose [hand] a barley-grain-shaped mark shines in the middle of the thumb shall be a man born on earth as an enjoyer of pleasures and prospers in happiness. (25) Meaning: If a barley-grain-shaped mark is clearly visible in the middle of one's thumb, that person shall be a happy enjoyer on this earth from birth until death. (28) And likewise: He in whose [hand] it is seen at the base of the middle and index fingers...

One shall be wealthy and enjoy happiness regarding children, wife, home, and so forth. (26) Meaning: If the shape of a *jīva* (a living being) is clearly visible at the base of the middle finger (*madhyamā*) or the index finger (*tarjanī*), that person will be wealthy, virtuous, honorable, and happy, becoming famous in the world and remaining content; he shall obtain the enjoyment of happiness through sons, wife, home, and the like. (26) And furthermore:

At the base of the ring finger (*anāmikā*) and at the preceding base of the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*), in that order, there is longevity for ten years; such is the statement of Sāmudrika. (27) **Meaning:** If, in the middle of someone's hand, [a mark] is at the base of the ring finger and the base preceding the little finger, [it indicates a lifespan of ten years]. This is accompanied by the *Bhāṣādīkā*.

If a curved mark is clearly visible, it should be known as the sign of a ten-year lifespan; such is the statement of the Lord reclining upon the Ocean of Milk. The essential meaning is this: if the life-line extends from the first part of the little finger up to the base of the first part of the ring finger, the sign of a life lasting ten years will be perceived in that life-line.

If several lines between the [major] lines are broken or slant downward, there will be the knowledge of drowning in water; if they ascend from above the life-line (āyurekhā) and slant downward, one will fall from a tree or a plantain tree; if the lines from the little finger to the index finger are incomplete, the lifespan shall be 120 years. || 27 || [The results of the upward lines: An upward line on the thumb is auspicious for a king.

He shall be a commander of armies, wealthy, and possess a middling lifespan. (28) Meaning: If an upward-moving line is seen rising above the thumb of a person, it should be known that he will become a most excellent sovereign of kings, a lord of a vast army, and wealthy; moreover, having lived for a middling lifespan—that is, fifty or sixty years—and having enjoyed all pleasures, that person [shall cast off his body] at a sacred pilgrimage site.

One should abandon [such a hand]. 28. And likewise: "If an upward line is seen extending as far as the base of the index finger (tarjanī), he shall become a royal messenger, and the destruction of his merit (dharma) arises. 29. Meaning: If an upward (vertical) line appears clearly reaching as far as the base of the index finger (the finger next to the thumb), it is a sign that one will become a royal messenger.

If a soldier, while wielding his sword, gains the authority to receive various kinds of intelligence (news) and yet his merit (*dharma*) is diminished—[this refers to] the breath [resulting from] the fasting of the thumb. 10. *Sāmudrika-śāstra*, with the commentary *Bhāṣāṭīkā*.

That is to say, by being fickle in performing royal duties throughout one's life, one becomes unstable; however, if there are lines at the base of the little finger, they grant the fruit of being devoid of effort toward the appropriate religious duties of one's own *varṇa* and *āśrama* due to the giving of initiation (*dīkṣā*). If there is one line, one becomes a donor and a benefactor; if there are two, after enjoying some slight sensual pleasure, one abandons the body. (29)

If there is one line, he will be virtuous, honorable, worthy of worship, and wise; and the vertical line is seen extending down to the middle base. If there are three lines, one attains great sovereignty, royal enjoyments, happiness, and prosperity; such a man is wealthy and happy, endowed with sons, grandsons, and other blessings. (30)

If there are four lines, one becomes highly learned, a scholar, wise, and intelligent—the meaning being that if there is an upward line reaching the base of the middle finger of the hand. If there are five lines, one becomes honored and established in the world. If six marks are visible and clearly perceived, that person will obtain happiness within their own lineage. If there are seven lines, one is considered an ordinary friend in the world.

33. He becomes fortunate, endowed with sons, grandsons, and so forth, wealthy, and happy; that is, having enjoyed pleasures and luxuries with great joy in this world for as long as he lives. If three lines are seen joined at the base of the little finger, he remains in happiness. 30. One, two, three, and the fourth joined with five (the "arrows"); 34. A line above the base of the ring finger indicates the acquisition of wealth through enterprise.

If three lines are clearly visible at the base of the little finger (the *kaniṣṭhā*) of one who possesses wealth (*artha*), then amidst worldly life, he shall live with both happiness and sorrow regarding his sons, grandsons, home, and so forth. [31] [The same applies to] one whose ring finger (*anāmikā*)—the finger adjacent to the little finger—possesses these lines. [This pertains to] the goals of life: Dharma, Artha, and Kāma.

One should understand these three lines as the signs for experiencing enjoyments (*bhoga*). If there is one line, or if it appears as a vertical line extending to the base, he will be successful in business—that is, he will become wealthy. If there are two lines, he will be righteous (*dharmātmā*). If there are three lines, he will be an enjoyer; through various kinds of endeavors, wealth will come to him, and through the lineage of sons, he will have four lines, becoming one who enjoys the company of many women. If there are five lines...

If a man, being joined with his wife, experiences some degree of happiness and sorrow within his home, he shall become wise, honorable, illustrious, and intelligent; he shall spend his life [with those women]. (31) As many lines as there are at the base of the little finger, for so many wives shall he enjoy pleasures and luxuries. If a line should exist on the path of the hand, situated at the root of the little finger—

If they come as far as this, and likewise if they reach as far as the lower base of one's own little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*), then those men indeed obtain a lifespan of a hundred years in their respective regions. (32) If these lines are seen to ascend upwards, they indicate the company of that many men. The meaning is: for one in whose hand there is an upward union at the root of the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*). (34)

If a line (*khaḍī*) appears clearly, a person with such lines will spend their life up to one hundred years, sustaining themselves within the world. [32] If a line is situated at the base of the index finger (*tarjanī*), it indicates strength of longevity; likewise, the lifespan shall be one hundred years, and death will be peaceful—of this there is no doubt. [35]

If lines are clearly visible at the base of the little finger (the youngest finger), they indicate honor and dishonor. From the marks of these lines, one gains knowledge of happiness, suffering, birth, death, and lifespan, as well as the granting of initiation, the path of righteousness, and happiness itself. (Sāmudrika-śāstra, with the Bhāṣā-dīkā commentary).

It is said that if one proceeds from the base of the little finger toward the middle of the hand—where two lines generally exist between the thumb and the index finger—and these two lines meet with the *āyur-lekhā* (life-line) at the base of the middle finger, the person shall live for one hundred years and pass their life in happiness. They say: if the two lines proceed from between the thumb and the index finger [and meet the life-line], [the lifespan is one hundred years].

Among them, if one line revolves from behind toward the middle of the hand, the lifespan will be seventy-five years. || 35 || Another line goes from the base of the little finger (kaniṣṭhā) up to the middle finger; this is seen as the line of longevity (āyū-rekhā). || 36 ||

If it meets the line and proceeds downward to remain there and becomes complete, know that he was born from his own father; however, if this [line] is incomplete, it signifies the destruction of the strength of the fourteen-year or twenty-four-year lifespan. (36) Meaning: If the *āyurekhā* (life-line), starting from the base of the little finger, reaches the middle finger without being incomplete, then one should know his birth to be from another [person].

Likewise, if two lines meet between the thumb and the index finger and are visible as far as the base of that finger, it should be understood that there was great affection between the mother and father; by adding fourteen and twenty-four together, [the total] is thirty-eight, and it should be said that his death will occur at thirty-eight years of age. (36)

One should know that there is no affection between the two; rather, quarrels and discord persist. If the line situated at the base of the ring finger (anāmikā) represents the father's life-force and it is short, slanting downward, then one should know his lifespan to be small—either ten years or sixty-three years—which destroys his vitality. (37)

If the lines are thick and red marks appear above them for the sake of the hands—if the *āyur-rekhā* (life-line) extends from the base of the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*) to the tip of the index finger (*anāmikā*), one should know that there is a long life. If the *mātṛ-rekhā* (mother-line) remains situated from [the base] up to the base of the ring finger (*anāmikā*), one should know the lifespan to be thirteen years.

If the line has gone upward from the side of the thumb and is endowed with a dark hue, it should be considered [as indicating longevity]; however, if only two lines are visible, one should know the lifespan to be sixty-eight years. (37) One should know that person's life to be short. If that same line is red in color and thick, it is a sign of death in childhood; but if it is full, one should know the mother’s life to be long. If the two lifespans of the mother and father appear deficient, they are respectively small, brief, or long.

If there is a trident (triśūla) in the upper portion in the middle of the lines, those men whose parents reside in heaven will experience happiness and sorrow; they shall die in childhood, without a doubt. (38) Having become gods, they shall go to the world of the gods. (39) Meaning: Regarding the consideration of the lines of the mother and father: if the line of life (āyu-rekhā) in one's hand is diminished, scanty, small, or large... [The remainder of the verse concerns the consideration of the lines of the mother and father.]

Likewise, if a line is seen at the waist, one should know that the lifespan will be short; those men in whom such a line is perceived will be possessed of both happiness and misery, and in their childhood state, they will undoubtedly meet with death. (38) Taking them one by one and in pairs, if a pair of lines is seen... (40) [This is] the characteristic of one born of adultery.

The lines of wealth (*artha-rekhā*) for the mother and the father are distinct from one another. The mother’s line runs between the forefinger (*tarjanī*) and the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*), meeting at the base of the fingers; whereas the father’s line is situated in the middle of the palm between the forefinger and the thumb. "The line arising from the father's lineage is a full line; a short line indicates the other's lineage. (39) *Sāmudrika Śāstra*, Chapter 14, accompanied by a vernacular commentary.

Emerging from the line of life and proceeding below it toward the left side of the hand (the western direction), it appears as if all the lines of the five fingers have merged together. If these become fifteen, that person becomes a great thief; such is to be known as the result of many lines. 40.

If sixteen lines are perceived upon counting, this is the "multi-lined" (*yūta-bahurekhā*) type; it indicates a small amount of hair, poverty, and low status. Such a person becomes a laborer—that is, a gambler—and a deceiver (a rogue). Furthermore, with these lines, one becomes a dwarf (*vāmana*); such is the word of the *Sāmudrika* [treatise] regarding happiness. (41) If there be seventeen lines, the person remains devoted to sinful deeds.

If there are eighteen lines, and many small lines between the lines of the mother and father, then he will be a righteous soul (44). If the lines appear short, one should know it as a sign of poverty; furthermore, if there are nineteen [lines], he will be honorable, a knower of virtues, and worshipped by the world—this should be understood. Likewise, if there are twenty [lines] between the lines of the mother and father, he will be known as an ascetic, and with twenty-one, a great soul (45).

If there are only a few lines, he will be somewhat impoverished yet enjoy some degree of happiness. The meaning is that one should know there to be nineteen lines on the five fingers of the right hand. This was described by the Lord who dwells in the Ocean of Milk to Śrī Brahmā. If these are clearly visible, that person will be honored by the world (attaining respect in the world). (41)

If twenty lines are clearly visible, he becomes a knower of virtues and honored by the world; if twenty-one lines are manifest, he is a great ascetic (tapasvī). Twelve lines bestow happiness and grant wealth and grain; such a person becomes a high-souled one (mahātman). (42, 45)

If the five fingers of a man's hand have distinct marks on the forehead, and if three lines each—totaling twelve—are clearly visible, then that person is to be known as one who enjoys wealth, grain, and other riches with ease; likewise, if the forehead is uneven due to large, shell-like protrusions resembling the crescent moon, he becomes wealthy even if previously poor. (42–46)

Regarding wealth: if one’s forehead is high and above it there are distinct lines visible like the shape of a conch shell, or if there is a crescent mark above the forehead, there will be great suffering and great affliction; such is the statement of the *Sāmudrika* [treatise on physiognomy]. (43)

If the lines on the forehead appear even, one will be born into a poor lineage; however, that man in whose hand all the lines of the five fingers are complete becomes very wealthy, happy, and an enjoyer of pleasures. 46. Furthermore: A forehead that is broad, high, elevated, and shaped like the crescent moon bestows sovereignty, while a forehead with great power grants the position of a preceptor. 47.

If a person’s forehead is broad, high, and large—resembling the crescent moon—and if such individuals number thirteen when counted, they are said by the Lord who reclines upon the ocean to be greatly distressed and possessed of manifold afflictions. (43) If there are fifteen lines on the forehead, one is a thief; at sixteen, a gambler and a deceiver; at seventeen, he should be known as a sinner; and at eighteen, he becomes a righteous soul. (44) 16. *Sāmudrika-śāstra* (The Science of Physiognomy)

Furthermore, if the forehead be large and as radiant as a conch shell, one should know that such a person is destined for the rank of an Ācārya. (47) Those whose foreheads are marked with prominent veins are always base and performers of sinful deeds; however, those with veins raised in the shape of a svastika are wealthy. (48) Meaning: A man on whose head the lines are situated with visible veins is inferior and a doer of evil acts; whereas one who possesses [veins] on his head...

If they possess high lines and resemble the *svastika* (auspicious cross), that man becomes wealthy. (18) Those with very short lines are inclined toward righteousness, while those with covered, indistinct, uneven, or depressed lines are devoid of wealth. Those with low lines are performers of cruel deeds and are subject only to bondage and death. (49) **Meaning:** Men with short lines are righteous; those with covered, indistinct, or unevenly elevated and depressed lines are poor.

Those who have low-pitched voices become bound, subject to execution, and performers of wicked deeds. (49) Three lines appearing on the forehead belong to those who live for a hundred years; for one with the strength of a bull, the lifespan is one hundred, or ninety-five. (50) Meaning: If three lines are clearly visible upon the forehead, one should know that his lifespan is one hundred years.

If four lines are clearly visible upon the forehead, one should know the lifespan to be ninety-five years. (50) With no lines, the lifespan is ninety; with broken lines, one becomes a wanton woman; and with lines reaching to the hairline, the lifespan shall be eighty. (51) Meaning: If there is not even a single line upon one's forehead, the lifespan will be ninety years.

If there are many lines on the forehead that are broken, fragmented, or crooked, that person remains intent upon committing adultery. Furthermore, if a single line is visible above the forehead at the root of the hair, his lifespan shall be eighty years. And forty years [are indicated] by thirty lines reaching the forehead. 52. Meaning: If ten lines (five on each side), or eleven lines (five and six), or fifty, or many lines are clearly visible on the forehead, the lifespan is forty years; furthermore, if one line appears curved above the forehead and extending over the eyebrows, the lifespan should be known with certainty as thirty years. 52.

If the lines on the forehead are twenty, crooked, or very small, his lifespan is twenty years. Alternatively, if the central line above the eyebrows—resembling the crescent moon—is visible on the left side of the forehead, his full lifespan is one hundred and twenty years. Or else... [53] Meaning: If the lines on the forehead are particularly numerous on the left side, or if they are crooked and very short, one should know that his lifespan is twenty years. Furthermore, if the central line above the eyebrows appears like the crescent moon, one should know that his full lifespan is one hundred and twenty years. Or else...

If there is no line above the brow, and it is neither as thick as the crescent moon on the second day of the lunar fortnight nor excessively thin—if it be exceedingly subtle, one should know that the lifespan will be very short. || 53 || A forehead that is auspicious, well-rounded in shape, free of hair, and pleasing to behold is a sign of kingship for men. || 54 ||

If a single line is clearly visible above the eyebrows on the forehead, and between the eyebrows there appears a mark mixed with hair, one should know that as the sign of being a king, as well as the signs for enjoying sovereignty and prosperity. (4) "If two lines reach the hairline, a man lives eighty years; if [the lines] are marked upon the forehead, he lives ninety years. (55) *Sāmudrika-śāstra*, Chapter 1, Verse 18, along with the commentary *Bhāṣā-ṭīkā*.

If there are two lines reaching to the very ends of a man's hair, he will live for eighty years. For wealthy men, if there are five lines on the head extending toward the right side, his life shall last for ten thousand years. If the forehead is endowed with many lines and the eyebrows are curved, it should be known as a giver of happiness; and if that [forehead] is full, this person shall sustain life for nine years. (56)

If the chin (*vāī*) is bent inward, one should know it to be indicative of suffering. (59) A protruding chin belongs to those who are destitute; a skull-like chin belongs to the long-lived; and a foolish person has a flat chin. This is the description of the form and color of the face. A very long chin belongs to those who possess suffering, while a flattened chin belongs to those who have killed their mother or father. (56) That man whose lotus-face resembles the face of his mother is generally a fortunate person; this was said by the Ocean. (60)

The head of men devoid of wealth is uneven (high and low). A man whose lotus-face resembles his mother’s face possesses a skull-shaped head and is long-lived; he is generally fortunate (happy, enjoyer of pleasures, and illustrious), as described by the Ocean. Furthermore, it has been stated that a very long head belongs to men who experience suffering. (60)

The head of a man who kills his mother or father becomes flattened and conical (ṭāsā). ||56|| For those who enjoy full sovereignty, the head resembles that of a lion or an elephant. ||61|| Even if the body of men or women is devoid of flesh, it may be slender. ||[62]||

That person whose face is round on all sides, terrifying, large, and covered with prominent veins should be known as extremely inauspicious. [17] However, those men or women whose limbs are smooth, beautiful to behold, symmetrical, and fragrant—provided they are well-fleshed like a lion or an elephant—are destined to rule a kingdom. Conversely, those who are thin, harsh, and have visible, glistening veins...

Indeed, the faces of those who enjoy all kinds of auspicious prosperity are exactly like this. (61) It should not be understood [otherwise]. (27) The face of the fearful is such; that of those devoid of sons is low and crooked. Before examining the lifespan, the physical characteristics of men must thus be known. A long [face] is to be known as belonging to the destitute, while a circular one belongs to the fortunate. (62) For in this world, the knowledge of physical characteristics is useless for those whose lifespan has been exhausted. (58) Meaning: The face of sinful persons is terrifying.

The mouth of a man who is childless is downward-turned and crooked; likewise, the mouth of those who are destitute is downward-turned and crooked. One should discern these characteristics through the knowledge of the *rākhā* (the line of fate): for those whose lifespan is exhausted, it is long, while the mouth of fortunate men is round. (62)

Knowing the physical characteristics (lakṣaṇa) is useless; that is to say, for a man of very short life, even the characteristics become false—such as a woman's face being broad for those who are childless. (58) A square face belongs to rogues, while an excessively long face belongs to misers. (63) For the fortunate, a head with five fingers (folds) and curling to the right leads to great happiness. Meaning: One should know that he whose face is broad is unfortunate.

Generally, for men, that which turns counter-clockwise leads to misery; furthermore, this [is the case]... 59. One whose face resembles a woman’s face should be known as childless. *Sāmudrika-śāstra*, with a vernacular commentary. One whose face is square should be known as a rogue (*māyāvī*); moreover, one who is hairless at the locus of the auspicious crescent moon shall meet death. One whose face is small should be known as a miser (*kṛpaṇa*). 63. Description of the lips.

The ears should be hairless, symmetrical, soft, and well-proportioned. (67) Meaning: Those whose two ears are like the moon on the second day [of the lunar fortnight], and whose lips are reddish and excellent; whose face is elevated, soft, and even, and free of hair; whose teeth are beautiful, dark, and even; and whose speech is like the sound of a crow—such ears are to be known as bestowing auspicious results. (67)

O friend, if one's lips are bright red, know that the result will be excellent; and if the upper flesh of the lips is wrinkled and the face is round, it is excellent. [Lips] that are oily, blue-black, and soft belong to fools, while those that are crooked and harsh [indicate] a poor result. If one's teeth are white in color like jasmine flowers, it is known as the most excellent fruit for women on the head, as well as on the feet and the palms of the hands. (68) Know this to be an excellent result.

Whose speech is like the melody of the cuckoo. Meaning: That man whose hair is glossy, black, soft, wavy, and thick should be known as possessing the best fruit; that is, these characteristics are to be understood as bestowers of happiness. (6) If it is like the hair on the heads of women, it should be known as excellent. Furthermore, [speech] endowed with courtesy, free from deceit, like the sound of a swan, and bringing comfort.

If the nostrils are even on the upper part of the face or on the palm—that is, the back of the hand—as previously described, they are known to bestow excellent results for women; indeed, such a nose is beautiful and auspicious. (65–68) Meaning: A woman whose mouth turns clockwise (toward the right) becomes wealthy, while one with lips as red as the *pāṭala* flower becomes possessed of wisdom. (69)

If one possesses great affection (tender), has a voice like that of a swan, and his lips are as red as coral, such a man generally attains a kingdom; he becomes a bestower of happiness. Furthermore, if a man’s nose is high and its nostrils are red like a bimba fruit, one should know that it yields auspicious results. If the face of a woman is beautiful, she becomes wealthy.

A man with lips having a color like the flower of the rose (gulāba) should be known as auspicious. || 6 || He becomes wise; and one with lips as red as the color of coral (munga) [attains prosperity]. One whose eyes resemble the blue lotus (nīlotpala), and whose nose is long and prominent, generally attains a kingdom. || 69 || Nor should the eyebrows on the forehead be like the broad crescent moon. || 66 || A man with full lips will be fortunate, while one with drooping lips is a partaker of enjoyments.

One whose two eyes are like blue lotuses attains wealth. One with very thick lips or thin and trembling lips becomes miserable. (70) Furthermore, the eyes reaching as far as the nose should not be excessively long. One whose lips are thick is a man of good gait and conduct, yet he remains poor. The eyebrows should not be like the crescent moon of the second day, but rather like a bow.

A man whose lips are long is an enjoyer of pleasures; if a beautiful frown appears upon his forehead, it yields most excellent results. Those whose lips are uneven (harsh) and do not look pleasing are timid. The underlying meaning is that whichever limb appears beautiful, well-proportioned, or terrifying to behold, it serves to identify the person—for instance, such a person would be a coward.

A man with small lips is unhappy. || 70 || If they are large, they bring about the rise of fortune and make one happy. || 66 || *Sāmudrika-śāstra*, with its commentary (*Bhāṣāṭīkā*): Characteristics of the Teeth; Characteristics of the Tongue. By thirty-two teeth one becomes a lord of men; by being deprived of even one of these, men become devoid of purity and right conduct, and their tongues remain white. By twenty-nine teeth one possesses little wealth; by twenty-eight, a man is happy. || 71 ||

Those with thirty teeth are devoid of wealth; those with black tongues have fallen into sin; and those with variegated tongues are of mixed character. (7) A man who possesses thirty-two teeth becomes a king. If a man has only twenty-nine teeth, he is constantly engaged in searching for wealth. Furthermore, one who has thirty teeth is destitute of mental power, and one whose tongue is black is devoid of riches.

A man who possesses eighteen teeth becomes wealthy; likewise, those men whose tongues are variegated with many colors are happy. Those who have nineteen teeth are always vessels for the suffering of poverty. Those whose tongues are red, long, thin, soft, and equal in size to the body, even if they lack one tooth, are happy. Those who lack twenty teeth are miserable. (71–72)

Those whose tongues are red in color, long, thin, and soft, eat sweet food; or else, they become speakers of the three Vedas. (76) A person whose twenty-nine *dūtis* (tongue-folds) move is poor and miserable; moreover, if even fewer than that move, such a person becomes wealthy. Furthermore, those whose teeth move [in a certain manner] eat sweet food, or they become speakers of the three Vedas. (76)

Characteristics of the Palate: A man whose reddish-brown palate is like a jasmine bud, even, very thick, and red like the interior of a lotus, becomes a courageous lord of the earth. Teeth that are glossy, not too sharp, and with prominent canines [indicate] a person endowed with splendor. 73. One with a white palate is rich in wealth; one with an elephant-like palate becomes a sovereign of a circle of territories. 77.

A man whose teeth are like the buds of the *artha-kundakī* flower, or whose palate is like a red lotus in its center, becomes a powerful and majestic king with a beard as thick, glossy, clear, and radiant as a red cinnabar; whereas one whose palate and teeth are white becomes a wealthy man. (73)

One who has such [palate] becomes wealthy; one whose palate is like an elephant's becomes a lord of a circle (maṇḍaleśvara). If the two teeth known as the "king-teeth" (rājadanta) appear first in the twelfth month after birth, they are auspicious. Similarly, those that are elevated at birth are auspicious. One with a reddish palate is endowed with virtues; the uvula (ghaṇṭikā) is auspicious when it is sharp-tipped, thick, and firm.

If the lower teeth appear within one year [of birth], such a person is long-lived; however, a tongue that is black, hard, thin, and flat is not auspicious for men. (78) The meaning is: he whose palate is red in color is virtuous; if his uvula is sharp and pointed, it is auspicious; but it should be known as inauspicious if the palate is thick, long, black, hard, and flat. (78)

Know that those with even teeth yield auspicious results; however, if the upper teeth appear within one year [of the lower ones], it should be known as inauspicious. Likewise, if two rows of teeth emerge simultaneously, that too is to be known as inauspicious. (74) [From the *Sāmudrika Śāstra*: Characteristics of the Nose] One with a prominent nose is fortunate; one with a nose like that of an elephant will be happy, wealthy, and possessed of great riches. One with a straight nose is endowed with enjoyments and lives a long life, whereas one with a dry nose will be [destitute]. (79)

That man whose nose is prominent has excellent gait and conduct; he whose nose is like the trunk of an elephant is happy and very wealthy; and he whose nose is dry lives for a very long time. (79) A man with a nose like a sesame flower becomes a king; one with a parrot-like nose becomes a ruler of the earth; one with a nose like that of an osprey is fierce and eloquent; and one with a short nose is foremost in character and righteousness. (80)

A person whose nose resembles a blooming *tilaka* flower or a parrot (*śuka*) becomes a king; one with a crooked nose is wealthy, and one with a small nose is devoted to virtue and righteousness. || 80 || Those who possess eyes resembling the color of a pearl necklace or yellow orpiment (*haritāla*) certainly become universal emperors (*cakravartin*); those with eyes like the petals of a blue lotus become proud and resentful men. || 81 ||

Those whose eyes are like the color of *haritāla* (orpiment) become universal monarchs (*cakravartin*); those whose eyes are like the petals of a blue lotus become learned and honored men. || 81 || One with eyes like an elephant becomes a commander of the army, while one with very long eyes becomes a spy. [Included as requested: Bhāṣāṭīkā-sahitam]

One whose eyes are long and wide lives for a very long time; he whose eyes are like those of a pigeon is a man of passion. (82) One becomes a king with eyes red as lac, a knower of the scriptures with eyes white like pearls, and a man of great wealth with tawny eyes like honey or gold. (83)

A person whose eyes are as red as the color of vermilion becomes a king; one whose eyes are white like the color of clay becomes a knower of the scriptures; and one whose eyes are yellow, resembling the color of honey or gold, becomes very wealthy. Those with many years of age have smoky-colored eyes, while those with few years of age have prominent eyes.

Those men whose eyes are smoky-colored are long-lived; those whose eyes are drooping have short lives; and those whose eyes are squinted or round do not transcend youth—that is, they pass away while still in their prime. (84)

are attained. 84. Those with dark-brown eyes possess good fortune; those with glossy eyes become great enjoyers of pleasures; those with wide-set eyes possess intelligence; and those with sunken eyes are destitute of wealth. 85. Meaning: A man whose eyes are smoky-grey becomes fortunate; a man whose eyes are glossy becomes a consumer of many enjoyments.

A man whose eyes are thick (prominent) is wise, whereas a man whose eyes have a dejected look is destitute of wealth. (85) One who has wide eyes is fortunate, and one with eyes like those of a pigeon is lustful. (82) [Note: The numbering appears to follow a specific sequence. Meaning: A man whose eyes resemble those of an elephant possesses an army; and one whose eyes are very large possesses long life. (From the *Sāmudrika-śāstra*).

One with a snake-like gaze is a sickly person; one with a cat-like gaze is always sinful. One with a cruel gaze is wicked, while one with a cock-like gaze is fond of strife. (86) Meaning: A man whose gaze is like that of a snake becomes diseased; one whose gaze is like that of a cat is perpetually a sinner.

Likewise, a person whose gaze is fierce (terrifying) is wicked; one whose gaze is like that of a cock is fond of quarreling—that is, he takes pleasure in fighting. ||86|| A blind man and one who is one-eyed are cruel, meaning they possess a wicked nature; a man who is even more one-eyed than a one-eyed man is more cruel still, and one who is timid becomes even more cruel than one who is both one-eyed and squinting. ||87|| Meaning: A blind man and a one-eyed man are cruel, that is, they are of a wicked disposition.

One who repeatedly rolls his eyes is more cruel than a one-eyed man; and one who steals the eye [of another] is even more cruel (wicked) than both the one-eyed and the one who rolls his eyes. (87) Those with owl-like eyes are extremely wicked; those with uneven eyes are to be known as miserable; those with swan-like eyes are devoid of wealth; and men with tiger-like eyes are prone to anger. (88)

Those men whose eyes are like those of an owl or a bird are exceedingly wicked; those whose eyes are irregular—that is, one larger than the other—are miserable; those whose eyes are like those of a swan are destitute of wealth; and those whose eyes are like those of a tiger are prone to anger. Those with eyes that are excessively tawny, discolored, or wandering are inauspicious.

Men whose eyes are excessively small, reddish, unattractive, rolling, and flickering do not fare well; furthermore, those whose eyes are very small, red, dry, moist, and dirty are poor men. (89) [The Characteristics of the Eyebrows] *Bhāṣā-ṭīkā-sahitam* (With Hindi Commentary): The characteristics of the eyebrows.

Men with eyebrows that are elevated, beautiful to behold, and clear become wealthy and possessed of sons; conversely, those with eyebrows that are low and unsightly become destitute of wealth, happiness, and offspring. (90) [The Characteristics of the Ears]

The first [type] has long ears and is happy; one with naturally thick and soft ears is wise; one with mouse-like ears is a king; and one with conch-like ears shall be a lord of the earth. (91) Meaning: If a person’s ears are long, naturally supple, and thick, that person attains happiness in the first stage of life.

A person whose ears are like those of a mouse is intelligent; one whose ears are like a conch shell becomes a commander of an army. || 91 || Those with short, sunken, or fleshless ears should be known as having an evil death; those with prominent veins are snake-bearers, and those with generally crooked ears are usually heroes. || 92 ||

If a person's ears are small and fleshless, they will be poor, destitute of wealth, and subject to death from sinful diseases or will themselves be sinful. Those whose ears are long, fleshy, and crooked generally become deceitful (of wicked nature). || 92 || One with flattened ears is an enjoyer of pleasures; one with long ears and hairy ears is long-lived. One with very thick ears becomes a great enjoyer, and one with large ears becomes a leader of men. || 93 ||

A person whose ears touch his shoulders is fortunate; one who has large hairs on his ears is long-lived. One with very thick ears is highly blessed, a leader of men, and possesses great happiness. 93. [From the *Sāmudrika-śāstra*]. Characteristics of the Jaw (*hunū*).

In this world, the chin of the meritorious is round, fleshy, neither too long nor too short, well-proportioned, and soft; whereas that of the poor is excessively thin, long, or thick, and divided into two parts at its tip. (94) Meaning: In this world, the chin of those men who possess merit is round, filled with flesh...

Those whose chins are neither too large nor too small, but are soft and well-proportioned, are meritorious men; whereas those whose chins are very thin, excessively large, thick, or divided into two parts, are poor men. (94) The pair of jaws situated on both sides of the chin should be well-knit for men; a long jaw is praised, while the opposite is inauspicious. (95)

If the lips of men are joined at both sides, round, and well-proportioned, they should be known as bestowing auspicious results; however, if the lips are the opposite of this, they should be known as bestowing inauspicious results. (95) [The Characteristics of the Mustache] In this world, for men, the mustache [grows] with two hairs on the first day, ten on the second, and one more on the tenth, in due order. This is the classification of the mustache; its deformity occurs in the sixteenth year. (96)

If the mustache of men emerges within twenty years, or within twenty-one years, it brings forth valor; however, if it appears within sixteen years, know that it produces a corruption of valor. || 26 || [With the Bhopāṭīkā commentary] 29. Those who are devoted to the wives of others are thieves; those with reddish mustaches are actors; and those with thick nails [are likewise so]. || 29 ||

If the hair of the mustache and beard is reddish, those men are lovers of other women; and those whose nails are thick, rough, thin, cracked, and like lotus-petals, and who have abundant hair on their mustaches and beards, are actors or possess a nature like that of an actor. || 97 ||

Characteristics of the Cheeks: Those whose cheeks are sunken, devoid of flesh, with sparse whiskers and excessive hair upon them, are sinful, partakers of suffering, bereft of fortune, and servants to others. (98) Meaning: Those men whose cheeks are fleshless (sunken), whose mustaches are small, and who have an abundance of hair on their cheeks, are sinners; they experience misery, are devoid of luck, and become messengers for others. (98)

Those whose cheeks are elevated are happy; those whose cheeks are full of flesh are endowed with abundant enjoyments and happiness; and those men whose cheeks are as broad and firm as those of a lion or a lordly elephant are fortunate rulers of men. (99) **Meaning:** Those men whose cheeks are high are happy. Furthermore, those whose cheeks are fleshy—that is, well-filled—are complete enjoyers and happy; likewise, those whose cheeks are as broad and firm as those of a lion or an elephant [are blessed].

These two types of men are considered excellent. || 99 || [Characteristics of the Back] One with a veiny back attains poverty; one with a curved spine likewise; one with a hairy back suffers hardship; and one with a broad back experiences separation from kinsmen. || 100 ||

A person whose back is sunken and crooked attains poverty; one whose back is excessively hairy suffers from hardship; and one whose back is thick incurs the destruction of his brothers. (100) From the *Sāmudrika Śāstra*, with a vernacular commentary: 31. One with a back like that of a tortoise becomes a king; one with a back like that of a horse becomes a vessel of enjoyment.

One whose neck is large becomes an obstacle-maker in excellent undertakings; even one with a tiger-like back becomes a lord of wealth, prosperity, and the army. (101) That is to say, he ruins the work that has been accomplished. (104) Meaning: He whose back is like the back of a tortoise—that man [possesses] the line of the forehead of a king.

A man whose back is like that of a horse becomes a fugitive; however, by means of four distinct lines situated on the forehead, a man attains a lifespan of eighty years, sovereignty over the earth, wealth, and prosperity, as well as the status of a commander-in-chief. || 101 || 105 ||

A man on whose forehead four lines are clearly visible possesses the mark of a neck; he lives for eighty years and becomes a king. (108) One with a short neck is praised; one with a rounded neck is happy, wealthy, and fortunate. One who lacks lines on the forehead lives for twenty-five years. However, one with a shell-like neck (*kambugrīva*) becomes a sovereign ruler, protected by a royal umbrella and a parasol. (109)

His life shall be certain and all prosperities will arise instantly. 106. Furthermore, one whose neck is short should be known as excellent; and one whose forehead is devoid of lines has a lifespan of twenty-five years. One whose neck is round becomes happy, wealthy, and a possessor of enjoyments.

He becomes prosperous and quickly attains wealth; it is certain that one whose neck is like a *kambu* (conch) shall be known as a king ruling under a single umbrella. || 106 || By three auspicious lines of life, or even by one, [longevity is indicated]. One with a neck like a donkey or a camel will certainly be miserable; one with a neck like a crane (*baka*) will be a hypocrite. || 107 || [Their respective lifespans are] seventy, sixty, and forty years, in sequence. || 107 ||

One with a withered head and neck, or one with a crooked neck, is devoid of wealth. If there is only one line, or if it is forty [finger-breadths long], that person is a hypocrite (a heretic); likewise, one whose neck is withered and veiny lives for a full year. Similarly, a man who has a short and flat [line] is devoid of wealth. This is certain. One with a buffalo-like neck is a hero, while one with a long neck is always a glutton. Alternatively, if there are three horizontal lines on the forehead, he shall live for a hundred years.

One with a crooked neck is a slanderer; one whose teeth are destroyed has a large neck. For those born on earth, however, there are four [types]; furthermore, the lifespan is one hundred minus five [ninety-five years]. 108. Meaning: He whose neck is like that of a buffalo is a warrior; or he upon whose forehead there are three large, slanted lines is a warrior; and he whose neck is long is a great eater. His lifespan should be known as one hundred years, provided [the other marks] are four.

If there are lines [on the forehead], one should know the lifespan to be ninety-five years. || 108 || Furthermore, he whose neck is crooked becomes a slanderer. According to the *Sāmudrika-śāstra*: "If the lines have reached the hairline, one lives for eighty years; by means of a line on the forehead, a man lives for ninety years, provided he is marked with many lines. || 109 ||

A man whose forehead has a single line extending to the ends of his hair lives for eighty years; likewise, he whose head is marked with many lines lives for ninety years. (109) If there are seven lines on the forehead, his lifespan is seventy years; if five more are situated at the tip, it is sixty years. If there are many lines, they grant men half a hundred [fifty] years, or even ten years less, as they are fragile. (110) The meaning is: if there are five lines on the front part of the forehead, that man—

One lives for seventeen years, or else one sustains life for sixty years. Those men upon whose foreheads there are many lines live for fifty years; however, if those same five lines are present, the lifespan shall be less than fifty, namely forty years. || 110 || A person whose forehead is joined by a pair of eyebrows lives for thirty years.

Furthermore, if there are lines above both eyebrows that are curved, he lives for twenty years. (111) If those same lines are broken, the man approaches women who should not be approached; if they are even minute, the man is short-lived.

"By means of lines, a man [attains his status]," so said Sumantu, the best of Brahmins. (112) The meaning is: he whose forehead has broken or fragmented lines is one who sports with women who should not be approached—that is, with improper women—and he whose forehead has short lines is a man of short lifespan. Thus did Sumantu, the foremost of the twice-born, describe the lines of a man along with their significance.

Regarding the characteristics of the shoulders: he whose shoulders are crooked, drooping, devoid of flesh, hairy, and thin—by such a lack of auspicious marks, even the name of Fortune (*lakṣmī*) has never been heard by him; he shall be so destitute that he does not even hear the name of wealth. (113)

Those whose shoulders are like those of a bull, fleshy, and free from fat, are carriers of burdens for men; however, those whose two shoulders are crooked, thin, very small, and excessively hairy are known to be causes of distress (or sorrow). 114.

The shoulders of two heroes who possess a well-knit skeletal structure should be somewhat elevated above the arms. (115) [The Characteristics of the Arms]: The arms should be fleshy, with unbroken joints, well-knit, and broad.

O Lord of Kings, if a man’s two arms are rounded, fleshy, and reach down to his knees, he becomes a great monarch. (116) [The Science of Physiognomy] If a man’s two arms are somewhat thin or lean, yet symmetrical, well-developed, stout, and shapely, and they hang down as far as the knees, being round and robust—such a man is said to possess these results: he becomes a great king. (116) [Sāmudrika Śāstra] 3. Sāmudrika Śāstra.

Arms that are hairy and short bring poverty; however, those that are hairless, long like the trunk of an elephant, and lustrous bring happiness and are most excellent. (117) Meaning: If both arms are excessively hairy and short, such arms bestow poverty; but if the arms are hairless, as long as an elephant's trunk, and radiant, they bring about happiness. (117)

Characteristics of the Chest: A man with a firm chest is wealthy; likewise, one with a thick, fleshy, and hairy chest is a warrior (bhaṭa). One with a small chest is destitute, and a man with an uneven chest dies prematurely. Meaning: He whose chest is firm becomes wealthy; he whose chest is hard and covered in hair becomes a warrior; furthermore, he whose chest is small is poor, and he whose chest is uneven [suffers an untimely death].

Untimely death occurs, and that person becomes poor. (118) The Characteristics of the Breasts: Breasts that are round, very smooth, soft, and symmetrical are praised in men. Those that are asymmetrical, rough, and misshapen generally lead to suffering. (119)

In men, breasts that are round, smooth, soft, well-proportioned, and symmetrical are known to grant excellent happiness; whereas those that are uneven, sunken, misshapen, or unsightly are generally understood to bring suffering. (119) [With Hindi Commentary]

He whose abdomen (belly) is like that of a frog (*maṇḍūka*) becomes a king; he whose belly is like that of a bull enjoys dalliance with a courtesan; furthermore, a man with a round belly is happy, and a person with a belly like that of a fish or a tiger is fortunate. 120.

That man whose belly is symmetrical on all sides becomes exceedingly wealthy; furthermore, he whose belly resembles that of a lion attains the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin). (121) [Meaning: That person whose abdomen is even on every side becomes very rich; moreover, he whose abdomen is like that of a lion obtains the sovereignty of a universal monarch. However, this result should be understood as occurring specifically due to birth in a royal family.

Otherwise, one becomes wealthy and powerful. (121) One with a belly like a dog's is poor; one with a belly like a jackal's possesses a protruding belly. One who is sinful has a thin belly, while a thief who steals from deer-like people has a belly like Hara’s. (122)

O Artha, he whose belly is like that of a dog or a wolf is poor (destitute of wealth); he whose belly is like that of a jackal is cowardly; he whose belly is emaciated is sinful; and he whose belly is like that of a tiger is a thief. 122.

A person whose belly is like a cooking pot becomes poor; one whose belly is shaped like a jar remains forever unfortunate and miserable; and one whose belly is like a serpent becomes a servant who eats much. (123) [Meaning: He whose stomach is like a *piṭhara* (cooking pot) is destitute; he whose stomach is like a *ghaṭa* (water jar) is always wretched and unhappy; and he whose stomach is like a *bhujaga* (serpent) becomes a dependent who consumes great quantities of food.

One becomes a doer [of deeds]. 123. Characteristics of the Abdomen: One with a frog-like belly is a king; one with a bull-like belly enjoys the wives of others. One with a rounded belly is happy; one with a belly like that of a fish or a tiger is fortunate. 124. *Sāmudrika-śāstra*, accompanied by the Bhāṣā commentary. Characteristics of the Navel: Broad, well-fleshed, deep, and expansive is auspicious.

A person whose two hands are broad—that is, long and wide—and possess red-black nails like those of a gun-bearer, becomes wealthy. [127] A person whose hands are as dry as a tiger’s claws and devoid of flesh becomes destitute; likewise, one whose navel is broad and adorned with three folds in its center, yet is fleshy, becomes poor. [127]
He whose root of the hand is marked with three full lines that are very high, deep (profound), broad, and which curve to the right (clockwise) within the navel—such a person is a singer.

It is auspicious; that is to say, a man with such a navel attains happiness, sovereignty, and wealth endowed with gold and jewels, just as a woman full of desire resorts to her husband (Śrīḥ pātāmava bhajati lubdhā). If it be otherwise than this, it should be known as inauspicious. 124. Meaning: He whose hand is endowed with three complete lines—that is, three... [the characteristics of the belly].

If the lines reach the end without being broken, extending from the base upward, that man generally suffers a fall into a deep pit. If a woman’s lower teeth are more numerous or larger than her upper ones, she will be motherless and remain miserable; if her teeth are misshapen—that is, ugly to look at—she will become a widow; and if her teeth are sparse (set far apart with gaps between them), she [will likewise suffer].

A woman who has a wandering tongue (is unchaste) [28]. Characteristics of the Tongue: A tongue that is soft, straight, red, and white is auspicious; one that is thick, narrow in the middle, or deformed brings about the destruction of happiness [29].

(31)

The characteristics of the abdomen: When a woman has a large belly, she gives birth to many sons; one with a frog-like belly [gives birth to a son who is] a lord of men, and one with a long and protruding belly [gives birth to] a powerful [son]. 78. Meaning: A woman whose belly is large gives birth to many sons, and if the belly is long and expanded, her son will be strong. 78. By means of a raised belly, a woman becomes barren.

With a protruding belly she becomes barren; with a hard belly, she becomes the wife of a Bhinduka. (79) With a belly marked by a whirlpool, she certainly becomes a maidservant. With sides that are soft, fleshy, and symmetrical, there is auspiciousness. (80) [Accompanied by the *bhāṣādīkā*].

O King, if there is a depression in the woman's belly, she will certainly be a servant; however, if the belly is soft, fleshy, and the sides are symmetrical, it yields auspicious results. (80) She whose belly is smooth-skinned and free of veins will have sons; she whose belly is very thin will be a passionate woman. Cherished with manifold enjoyments, she will daily eat sweetmeats and excellent fruits. (81)

O Noble One, that woman whose abdomen is devoid of veins, soft, and covered with fine skin—or even if she is very thin—becomes the mother of sons; she has a longing for various kinds of incomparable enjoyments, and she daily consumes excellent sweets (such as *modakas*) and fruits, nuts, and other such items. (81) Furthermore, her abdomen is shaped like a water-pot (*ghaṭa*) and resembles a *mṛdaṅga* drum.

Even that which is devoid of a son, brought about by fate, and lacking in auspiciousness—though it may appear like a gourd, it is described by those who know the truth as being equal to a hard, large *śāla* tree. (82)

Regarding the meaning: if a woman’s belly is shaped like a jar, or like a drum, or by the power of fate like a grain of barley, that woman will be destitute of sons; likewise, if the belly is shaped like a water-pot (kumbha), it does not yield auspicious results. Furthermore, if the thighs are as hard as a palmyra tree (śāla), those who know the truth have described the result to be similar to what was previously stated. || 82 || [The Characteristics of the Navel]

A navel that is deep and spirals to the right increases one's fortune; however, one that is prominent, knotted, flat, or spirals to the left is not auspicious. (83) **Meaning:** If a woman’s navel is deep and turns toward the right, it brings about the increase of prosperity; whereas a navel that is visible, knotted, elevated, or turning to the left is not beautiful. (83) [With the Bhāṣā-Ṭīkā]

If the vulva (*bhaga*) of a woman is as well-formed as the shoulder of an elephant or shaped like the back of a tortoise, she will be a queen who brings joy through amorous play with the king; furthermore, a woman whose vulva is elevated above is one who gives birth to daughters, according to the *Sāmudrika-śāstra*.

A navel that appears with a prominent fold in the middle, or one that is open or twisted toward the left side, is not auspicious. (83) Regarding the characteristics of the hips and waist: She whose hips are well-elevated and whose waist measures eight fingers in breadth shall become the chief queen of a king, surrounded by many female attendants. (84)

O noble one, that woman whose hips are high and whose waist measures twenty-four finger-breadths shall become the chief queen of a king, perfectly endowed with many female companions; that is, she shall be a queen and many maidservants shall attend upon her. || 84 || A waist that is sunken, drooping, long, flattened, shaped like a cart, narrow, or covered in hair, indicates widowhood for a woman. || 85 ||

85. O King, if a woman’s waist is fleshy, bent, shaped like a cart-pole (gādī), narrow, and covered with many hairs, a woman with such a waist becomes a widow. 86. If women possess beautiful buttocks, they shall grant many enjoyments; those whose buttocks are well-raised, fleshy, and broad will always experience the pleasures of love.

Regarding the meaning: if the hips (*nitamba*) of fortunate women are as beautiful as the *bimba* fruit, they bestow great enjoyment; and if they are high, thick, and large, those women always grant the pleasure of desire—that is, such hips are excellent. (86) The Characteristics of the Vagina (*yonilakṣaṇa*): When the vulva (*bhaga*) has a form like the shoulder of an elephant, or like the back of a tortoise, or like that of a bull; or when it is elevated on the left side, it grants the husband of the earth the diversion of love.

He too becomes a father of sons. (87) He becomes a bali. (87) Or, the vulva (*bhaga*) that has the form of an *aśvattha* leaf, or one with a hidden jewel (*gūḍhamaṇi*), is auspicious; likewise, that which has the shape of the interior of a hearth or resembles the hoof of a deer. (88) Meaning: That vulva of one's own which is shaped like a *pipala* leaf, or which is like a hidden jewel, is auspicious; as well as that which is like the belly of a hearth or like the hoof of a deer. 89. A vulva that is covered with excessive hair such that the birth-canal is not visible, and whose mouth is distorted—that is known as the lowest type; it does not serve as a source of pleasure for lovers in any way whatsoever. *Artha:* Likewise, one should know that a vulva which is so thickly covered with hair that the birth-canal cannot be seen, and whose opening is distorted—meaning it does not appear attractive—is the lowest type; it is by no means a cause of joy for a man of passion.

The vulva of a woman that has the shape of a bodice (kañcukāvarti)—meaning it is elevated on both sides and hollow in the middle—is a cause for increasing misfortune; even if it is curved in shape, it is likewise incapable of conceiving a fetus. (90) **Meaning:** If a woman's vagina is *kañcukāvarti*—that is, high on both sides with a depression in the center—such a vagina increases one's ill fortune.

Furthermore, she who is unfit for conception, or whose vulva (*bhaga*) is curved in shape, should be known as one who increases misfortune and is incapable of bearing children. (90) From the *Sāmudrika-śāstra*: A vulva that resembles the leaf of the cane or bamboo, or has the appearance of camphor, is auspicious; however, one that is long-necked, deformed, hairy like an elephant, or flat is declared to be inauspicious. (91)

O King, if a woman’s vulva is shaped like a bamboo leaf or a reed leaf; or if it is deep in the middle, high on one side, and like a throat—wide on one side, long and high on the other, and low on the third; and if the hair upon it resembles that of an elephant, and her vulva is flattened—such a vulva should be known as inauspicious. (91) However, if the hips are exceedingly soft and covered with a cluster of very tender hairs, then that vulva is a vessel of fortune.

Moreover, that which is elevated, extensive, and resplendent is described by the wise as being graced with the art of a husband through devotion. (92) Meaning: If a woman's vulva (*yoni*) is very soft and endowed with soft body hair, it bestows sovereignty; likewise, if it is elevated, large, and radiant—that is, luminous—it is also a vulva that increases the heart's longing through the respectful art of a husband, such that one’s mind is uplifted by looking upon or touching it.

The wise have declared that which increases one's sovereignty. (92) At that very time, a [yoni] that spirals to the right, is fleshy, and indicates auspiciousness; however, one that is excessively thick and has a great opening brings about misfortune immediately. (93) Meaning: If a woman’s yoni spirals to the right and is thick, it is auspicious; but if it spirals to the left or is as if broken in some place, such a yoni makes women unchaste. (93)

A vulva that is sunken, crooked in shape, and rough indicates widowhood; one that is excessively thick and very long causes immediate misfortune. (94) [With the Bhāṣā-ṭīkā: The meaning is: if a woman’s vulva is devoid of flesh, somewhat curved, and rough, it should be known as indicative of widowhood—that is, it makes her a widow; and if the vulva is very thick and very long, it becomes a cause of immediate lack of fortune. (94)

A vulva that is soft, broad, beautiful, and elevated is auspicious; however, one that is marked by lines, veiny, or covered with hair yields inauspicious results. (98) She whose vulva resembles a conch shell does not conceive a child here in this world. A vulva elevated on the left side indicates the birth of a daughter, while elevation on the right side indicates the birth of a son. (96)

O noble lady, if a woman’s vulva is coiled like a conch shell—bulging on one side and narrow on the other—such a vulva does not conceive. Furthermore, if a woman’s vulva is elevated toward the left, daughters are born; if it is elevated toward the right, sons are produced. (96) Her shanks are like plantain stems, hairless and rounded.

If her thighs are fleshy, symmetrical, smooth, and glossy, she will certainly become a queen. (97) Regarding the characteristics of the knees: If the pair of knees is fleshy, perfectly rounded, and very auspicious, it bestows great fortune.

In this treatise on the science of bodily marks (*sāmudrika-śāstra*) composed by Ādibhī for the delight of the Lord of the World, this [verse] describes the "reverse" (*viparīta*). Meaning: If both knees of a woman are thick, very round, and possess well-defined joints, they bestow highly auspicious results; such a woman becomes like the consort of a great king (*mahārāja*). However, if her knees possess characteristics contrary to those previously described, she should be known as having "reverse" qualities. (98) [The following is] the description of the hair (*roma-lakṣaṇa*).

A woman with a single hair at each hair-follicle (*romakūpa*) on her calves is beloved by a king; one with two hairs at each is a partaker of happiness; and one with three hairs at each should be known as a widow. 99. [The Characteristics of the Hands] **Meaning:** If there is only one hair at the root of each hair-follicle on a woman's calves, she becomes the beloved of a king (a queen); if there are two hairs at each, she becomes a partaker of happiness (possessing prosperity); and if there are three hairs at each, she becomes a widow. 99. [The Characteristics of the Hands]

A woman with even ankles is fortunate, while one with broad ankles is unfortunate. A woman with high ankles is unchaste, and one with long ankles is afflicted by disease. (100) [The Characteristics of the Ankles] **Meaning:** A woman whose knees are symmetrical and beautiful is blessed with good fortune; however, if her knees are high, she becomes an unfaithful wife. A woman whose ankles are always fleshless certainly becomes unfortunate. However, if both ankles are well-concealed, free of visible veins, round, and beautiful, she will be fortunate—that is, endowed with excellent prosperity. (101) Meaning: If a woman's two ankles—the parts below the knees—are devoid of flesh, meaning they are dry and thin, that woman will inevitably be unfortunate. Conversely, if both ankles are thick, veinless, round, and beautifully well-nourished, she will be fortunate, meaning possessed of great wealth and status.

...is so. 101. [End of] Bhoja’s Commentary. 81. Those whose ankles are exposed and flaccid are indicators of misfortune.
