Characteristics of the Feet: Like a lotus, a conch, a chariot, a banner, a discus, a broad fish, or a canopy.

If there are marks upon the feet of women resembling a lotus, a conch, a chariot, a banner, a discus, a large fish, a celestial vehicle, or moonlight, she becomes the consort of kings—meaning, that woman whose feet bear the aforementioned marks becomes a queen, endowed with sovereign power. (103)

[This] is appropriate. 103. Characteristics of the Soles of the Feet: It is said that the sole of a young woman’s foot is tender, even, and possesses the luster of a *japā* flower; it bestows upon the lord of the earth great prosperity, abundant merit, and freedom from disease. 104.

O King, that woman whose soles are soft, even, and red like the *japā* flower is wealthy, hot-tempered by nature, beloved by her husband, yet largely devoid of virtue. (104) A woman's soles that are shaped like winnowing baskets, discolored, parched, rough, or likewise masculine in appearance, indicate misfortune. (105)

If a woman’s toes are interlaced with one another, she will kill many husbands and become a *vāravāmā*—that is, a prostitute—in this world. (107) The characteristics of the ring finger (*anāmikā*) and the middle finger (*madhyamā*): If both the ring finger and the middle finger do not touch the ground, [she is a prostitute]. (108)

The first [type] destroys two husbands, while the other destroys three husbands. (108) — *Artha*: If the ring finger and the middle finger of a woman's feet do not touch the ground and one of them remains raised, she destroys two husbands; if both remain raised, she destroys three husbands and becomes an adulteress. (108) "If the ring finger and the middle finger are found to be deficient [in touching the ground], then she shall be deprived of her husband," so the Blessed One himself has said. (109)

If the ring finger (the finger next to the little finger) is shorter than the middle finger between the feet, that woman will be unfaithful to her husband; this was described by the Blessed One himself. (109) [With the commentary]. The Characteristics of the Little Finger: If the little finger of a woman does not touch the heel, then she, having quickly killed her own husband, will sport again with a lover. (110)

Meaning—If, while walking, the little toe of a woman does not touch the ground, that woman will soon kill her husband and then take pleasure with other men. (110) The Characteristics of the Toes: If the toes of fawn-eyed women are glossy, rounded, and elevated, and are copper-colored, they bestow great enjoyment. (111)

Meaning: If the nails on the feet of a woman are smooth, rounded, raised, and resemble the color of copper, they bestow excellent enjoyments and sovereignty upon women. (111) The Characteristics of the Back of the Foot: If the back of the feet of deer-eyed women is indeed stainless and soft like the back of a lotus, and resembles the color of saffron, coral, or red lac, then it is certain that such a back of the foot possesses many virtues. (112)

If the soles of the feet of that deer-eyed woman are pure, soft, and red like the back of a lotus petal, or like saffron or coral, then that woman is certainly possessed of many virtues. || 112 || Other auspicious marks: A woman whose feet are always bent will be poor; one with prominent veins will be a traveler; and she who has an excess of hair [on her feet] will be a servant. || 113 ||

The meaning is this: if there is *natva* (depth) between a woman's feet, she is *jāda* (destitute); if there is *natva* on the tops of her feet, she is *sāmudrika-śāstra-gati-lakṣaṇa* (possessing the characteristics of movement described in the science of palmistry). When the stream of dust from a woman’s feet is forcibly kicked up onto the royal highway, that unchaste woman (*pāṃsulā*), having swiftly destroyed three lineages, always rejoices with wicked men. (106)

If a woman, while walking along a path, raises a cloud of dust, or if she walks by leaping with her own strength, she is called *pāṃsulā*, meaning an unchaste woman (*jāriṇī*). Such a woman quickly destroys three families—namely, those of her mother, father, and husband—and remains forever well-disposed toward wicked people. (106) The Characteristics of the Toes: If a woman's toes are interlaced with one another...

Having killed many husbands, she becomes a *vāravāmā*—that is, a prostitute—in this world. (107) The Characteristics of the Ring Finger and the Middle Finger: If the ring finger (*anāmikā*) and the middle finger (*madhyamā*) do not touch the ground, the former destroys two husbands, while the latter destroys three husbands. (108)

Regarding the meaning: if, among the toes of a woman's feet, the ring finger and the middle finger do not touch the ground while the other remains raised, it destroys two husbands; if both remain raised, it destroys three husbands and causes her to become an adulteress. O King, that deer-eyed woman whose soles are pure, soft, and red like the back of a lotus leaf, or like saffron or coral, is certainly possessed of many virtues. || 112 || Other auspicious marks: A woman whose ankles are prominent suffers from poverty; through their being low, she is always honored by noble men. That woman whose feet possess depth (firmness) between the toes and who is destitute of wealth due to being thin [in that area], and who has more than eight lines on her toes, is a traveler; likewise, she who has more than nine lines on her toes becomes a maidservant. || 113 || Furthermore, she whose little toe and ring finger do not touch the ground...

If the big toe goes beyond the fore-toe, she is an unchaste woman. (114) Meaning: That woman whose little toe and ring toe do not touch the ground while walking, or whose big toe rises up onto the adjacent fore-toe while walking, is an unchaste woman (vyabhicāriṇī). (114) If the two calves are elevated above those [ankles] and the shanks are excessively devoid of veins and firm, [she is auspicious].

Hairy, excessively dark, and pot-bellied—these are likewise [inauspicious]. (115) Meaning: Those women whose two thighs are very thick at the upper part, in whose thighs the veins are visible, who have excessive hair, whose flesh has increased excessively, and whose belly is shaped like a water-pot—these characteristics are not auspicious. (113) A navel that spirals to the left and a small private region belong to those who are miserable.

A woman whose navel is curved to the left and small, whose anus is also curved to the left and small, and whose neck is short while her vulva is large—such a woman remains miserable and her lineage comes to ruin. (116) There is no doubt that women who are stout and fierce will likewise meet with such fate.

If a woman’s cheeks are thick, she is fierce (prone to quarreling); and if her eyes are yellowish-brown, elongated, and flickering like those of a cat, a woman with such characteristics is certainly unchaste. 117.

If there are dark spots on her cheeks, that woman is certainly unchaste; and a woman whose forehead is elongated destroys her husband's younger brother (the *devara*). (118) Meaning: If a woman’s cheeks appear to have some dark-colored moles, that woman will inevitably be unfaithful. Furthermore, a woman whose forehead is long brings about the destruction of her husband’s younger brother; that is to say, the husband’s younger brother dies if the woman has a long head.

Indeed, those women whose limbs, such as the hands and feet, have many veins that are uneven and withered, become destitute of wealth, sorrowful, and devoted to sin; likewise, a woman who has upward-pointing veins on her head is a *ḍākinī* (a quarrelsome woman). 122. **Meaning:** If a woman’s hands, feet, and other limbs possess numerous veins, and if those veins are irregular and dry, that woman is devoid of wealth, afflicted by misery, and sinful; furthermore, a woman who has vertical veins (*ūrdhvanāḍī*) on her head is a *ḍākinī* (one prone to strife).

She becomes unfaithful (vyabhicāriṇī). (122) She who has a prominent upper lip, is quarrelsome, and has coarse hair—among women, these are defects; where there is beauty of form, therein lies virtue. (123)

Women are said to be of five types: 1. Padminī, 2. Citriṇī, 3. Śaṅkhinī, 4. Hastinī, and 5. Kṛtyā. In the *Kāmaśāstra*, four types of women are generally described, and their respective characteristics are also stated separately for each of those four. Likewise, five types of men are described along with their characteristics, namely: 1. Deva, 2. Gandharva, 3. Yakṣa, 4. Rākṣasa, and 5. Piśāca.

Therein, first the characteristics of women are described. The Characteristics of the Padminī: She whose face is like the full moon, whose eyes are like those of a deer, whose breasts are full, and who is virtuous; who is delicate, whose fragrance is like that of a blooming lotus, and who possesses either a dark or a fair complexion; who delights in little food, is skilled in amorous play, has a voice like a swan, and is fond of singing; who is modest and devoted to the worship of elders and gods—she is called a Padminī. (1)

She whose face is like the full moon, whose eyes are like those of a deer, and whose breasts are firm; she who is intelligent, soft-limbed, and possesses the fragrance of a blooming lotus; she who is dark or fair-complexioned, moderate in eating, skilled in the arts of love, whose voice is like that of a swan, and who sings; and she who is endowed with modesty and [devotion] toward her gurus and deities.

A woman endowed with these characteristics and devoted to worship is called a *padminī*. 1. The Characteristics of a *Citriṇī*: Dark-complexioned, lotus-faced, with eyes like those of a deer, slender-waisted, affectionate, knowledgeable in the science of music, beautiful-bodied, with prominent breasts, and artistic; fond of external conversation, possessing the gait of an elephant, her breasts smeared with excellent *kuṅkuma*—this intoxicated woman is described by the poet Mādhava as a *citriṇī*, who is like a painting. 2.

With high breasts, skilled in the art of painting, engaging in conversation here and there, possessing a gait like that of a young elephant, and adorned with saffron paste—Kavi Mādhava has described such a woman as a *citriṇī*, just as one speaks of a painting; that is to say, a woman possessing the aforementioned characteristics is called a *citriṇī*. ||2|| The Characteristics of a *śaṅkhinī*: One with slender limbs, crooked eyes, fine hair, and who increases the pleasure of sexual union.

Generally possessing long hair, naturally treacherous, and difficult to enjoy in sexual union; with reddish-brown and restless gait, she delights in worshiping her limbs with *barbara* grass; her body marked by nail-prints in various places—she is considered to be the *Śaṅkhinī*. (3)

A woman who has a subtle body, crooked eyes, small breasts, who increases the pleasure of amorous play, possesses long hair, has a wicked nature, is difficult to part with during the time of union, is tawny in complexion, has a restless gait, whose limbs are smeared with yellow sandalwood paste, and whose body is marked with nail-scratches in many places—such a woman is called a Śaṅkhinī. ||3||

The Characteristics of the Elephant-Woman (Hastinī): One who has a thick and broad chest, a very soft gait, a cruel disposition, a bent neck, slightly tawny hair, large breasts, and a face devoid of modesty; whose lips are like the *bimba* fruit, who has a craving for abundant food, who speaks harshly, and who delights in the scent of elephant ichor—she is considered an *Hastinī*.
